cim: Is it AI or SI? Neither seems fully right. | Opinion
cim_eredeti: Is it AI or SI? Neither seems fully right. | Opinion
szoveg_eredeti:
These days writing teachers are all a bit confused. They are trying to figure out what to do with AI programs like Claude and ChatGPT. Should students only be evaluated on in-class writing, so the instructors know their ideas and language are “authentic” rather than artificial? Or should they allow some use of AI for brainstorming? Perhaps only to fine-tune their papers? Or maybe to help with basic organization, or titling? What should the rules be?

It's first worth trying to define what “artificial intelligence” actually means. Ironically, the word “artificial” originally (14th c.) meant "of or belonging to art." Though over the next few centuries it evolved to mean “unnatural or contrived or insincere” — nearly the antithesis of the original meaning. The term “artificial intelligence” was first coined at a research conference at Dartmouth College in 1956. The underlying premise for the conference was that “every aspect of learning or any other feature of intelligence can in principle be so precisely described that a machine can be made to simulate it.” By then the “art” in artificial had become something very different — not a core human act of creative expression, but a mechanized simulation.

And that’s the point: Serious writers and teachers do view their subject as art, which means it requires paying careful attention to the world. And that has become much harder to do. We live in an always reeling, TikToking, Snapchatting world of perpetual distraction and shrinking attention spans, which is a challenge in the classroom. And, this frantic online world has also catalyzed a crazed longing for attention, for likes, for followers, for influence. So that is the question we all live in: How does one both fervently pay attention and desperately seek it?

Speaking of AI distractions: Oddly, the voice rec app on my phone just auto-corrected “artificial” to art official. But there is no such thing. Art, like beauty is not “official,” but immeasurable and intensely subjective. We all see things through the lens of our own experience. So maybe the term alludes to a person who judges which painting or sculpture or essay is most beautiful? Some sort of art expert? If so, surely that person would know that art is not artificial, but authentic and decidedly human.

President Donald Trump’s most recent response to the AI dilemma is to eliminate the word “artificial.” He realized that the word was distracting his supporters from his agenda. And he knows that most Americans see the problem rather than the promise in AI, and don’t want the enormous data centers polluting and displacing their communities. So in September he signed an executive order formally directing the federal government to replace "Artificial Intelligence" and "AI" with "Super Intelligence" and "SI" across all executive branch operations. On Truth Social he went on to say that anyone who used "Artificial Intelligence" instead of "Super Intelligence" will be considered “the enemy.”

So I guess I may be the enemy. Though the president seems more focused on the “social” rather than “truth” aspects of this issue, and not too concerned about what any of these words actually mean. Artificial Intelligence is now defined as “the capability of computer systems or algorithms to imitate intelligent human behavior” (Merriam Webster). The key word is imitation. It is human-made but not human. It does not involve consciousness or a conscience. In short, “artificial” is the correct word to describe AI and the technology in question.

“Super,” on the other hand, would seem irrelevant. It’s a prefix that evolved throughout the 20th century: heroes became superheroes, stars became superstars, and markets became supermarkets. But does adding “super” (i.e. “above or higher”) actually change the meaning of the noun it modifies? Perhaps, at times it has — to adapt to modernity. Some powerful countries were called superpowers, for example, only when they had acquired nuclear weapons. But that’s not the norm. The point is that “super” is not an accurate substitute for “artificial.” Rather, it is simply yet another strategic distraction. No different than calling authentic, well-researched news “fake news.” Or renaming the the Department of Defense “the Department of War.” Or claiming that Canada will be the “51st state.”

If the president is intent on using “super” to replace “artificial,” I would suggest he go with superficial intelligence. It’s a more accurate modifier, and suggests the paradox we are all living in.

Tom Montgomery Fate is a retired English professor who grew up in Iowa. His most recent book is "The Long Way Home," a travel memoir.
